description: Lunar Echoes is of curious, creative, and passionate minds ready to explore the mysteries of space through science, technology, and storytelling. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to tackle the challenge *“Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars”* by combining space exploration, coding, artificial intelligence, data analysis, and creative visualization.
summary:
LUNAR ECHOES is an interactive digital museum about the equipment humanity has left on the Moon and Mars. Since 1967, NASA has sent landers, rovers and science stations to both worlds. Most fell silent long ago, but they are still there, and one, the Apollo 11 laser reflector, is still used by scientists today.

The site is built around three pillars. Explore the Past: an archive of 12 objects with their missions, stories, last documented signals and a virtual museum. Investigate the Present: a Planetary Detective, a reasoning game that separates evidence from assumption, a heritage map on real NASA maps, and an image lab showing what NASA photos can and cannot tell us. Shape the Future: Rover Rescue, a rover-design simulator, real citizen-science projects (MoonDiff, Cloudspotting on Mars), ethics dilemmas, a landing-site designer and a time capsule.

Every fact is traced to NASA sources, mainly the challenge-listed NSSDCA catalogue, and is labelled Verified, Interpretation or Unknown. Nothing is guessed. This matters because abandoned hardware is part of our shared history and scientific record. As exploration grows, we need to understand what we leave behind and decide how to protect it.
details:
LUNAR ECHOES is an interactive digital museum about the hardware NASA has left on the Moon and Mars: landers, rovers and science stations, from Surveyor 3 (1967) to InSight (2018). It turns NASA's records into stories, investigations and decisions.

WHAT IT DOES

It follows three pillars:

1. Explore the Past: an archive of 12 objects with digital heritage passports (purpose, mission, science, fate, current status, sources), One Mission Four Perspectives (engineer, scientist, historian, future explorer), The Last Signal (each mission from launch to its last documented event) and a Virtual Planetary Museum with optional narration.

2. Investigate the Present: the Planetary Detective (sort claims into Confirmed, Interpretation, Possibility or Unknown), Evidence or Assumption?, the Forgotten Footprints heritage map on real NASA maps (verified, approximate and unknown locations), and the Mission Footprints Lab (NASA images with what they can and cannot tell us, including a matched HiRISE before/after of Phoenix).

3. Shape the Future: Rover Rescue (drive, sample and reason with clearly labelled simulated instruments), Build Your Own Rover, real citizen science (MoonDiff, Cloudspotting on Mars), ethics dilemmas, a Landing Site Designer (real distances to heritage sites and NASA's 2 km recommendation), a Planetary Time Capsule, a quiz and an Explorer's Logbook.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It teaches how scientists separate evidence from interpretation, shows that "abandoned" hardware still has scientific and historical value, and points visitors to real NASA citizen-science projects. Every fact is traced to a NASA source and labelled Verified, Interpretation or Unknown. Nothing is guessed.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript and JSON (no frameworks, no backend, no paid APIs), hosted on Vercel with code on GitHub. We also used Python for image preparation, headless Chrome for testing and Claude Code (AI) as a coding and research assistant.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

It combines a museum, a detective game and a decision simulator in one story. We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility (keyboard use, reduced motion, readable contrast, works on mobile), offline use, heritage ethics, and clear labelling of simulated and hypothetical content.
